intro_en:
# Before the first scene: reading Japanese

No audio or prior literacy is assumed. Keep it available beside the story. You can begin reading with the charts; you do not need to memorise them first.

Japanese normally runs without spaces. A kana sign represents a short rhythmic unit called a mora. Some sounds use two signs but still form one mora, such as きゃ (kya). English spellings below are reading aids, not English words. Japanese vowels are approximately a as in father, i as in machine, u with unrounded lips, e as in bed, o as in more without its final glide. English comparisons are approximate; text cannot supply a full pronunciation course.

## Hiragana

| | a | i | u | e | o |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| vowel | あ a | い i | う u | え e | お o |
| k | か ka | き ki | く ku | け ke | こ ko |
| s | さ sa | し shi | す su | せ se | そ so |
| t | た ta | ち chi | つ tsu | て te | と to |
| n | な na | に ni | ぬ nu | ね ne | の no |
| h | は ha | ひ hi | ふ fu | へ he | ほ ho |
| m | ま ma | み mi | む mu | め me | も mo |
| y | や ya | — | ゆ yu | — | よ yo |
| r | ら ra | り ri | る ru | れ re | ろ ro |
| w | わ wa | — | — | — | を o (particle) |

ん is its own mora, conventionally written n. Japanese r is a brief tongue tap, not an English r. Modern ordinary words do not require obsolete ゐ or ゑ.

Two small strokes, dakuten, change a consonant. A small circle, handakuten, changes the h row to p.

| | a | i | u | e | o |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| g | が ga | ぎ gi | ぐ gu | げ ge | ご go |
| z | ざ za | じ ji | ず zu | ぜ ze | ぞ zo |
| d | だ da | ぢ ji | づ zu | で de | ど do |
| b | ば ba | び bi | ぶ bu | べ be | ぼ bo |
| p | ぱ pa | ぴ pi | ぷ pu | ぺ pe | ぽ po |

じ and ぢ, and ず and づ, often have the same pronunciation in standard Japanese, but their spelling is not interchangeable. Preserve the spelling you read.

Small ゃ, ゅ, ょ combine with the preceding i-column sign: きゃ kya, きゅ kyu, きょ kyo. The main sets are きゃ/きゅ/きょ, ぎゃ/ぎゅ/ぎょ, しゃ/しゅ/しょ (sha/shu/sho), じゃ/じゅ/じょ (ja/ju/jo), ちゃ/ちゅ/ちょ (cha/chu/cho), にゃ/にゅ/にょ, ひゃ/ひゅ/ひょ, びゃ/びゅ/びょ, ぴゃ/ぴゅ/ぴょ, みゃ/みゅ/みょ and りゃ/りゅ/りょ. Thus きや is ki-ya, two morae; きゃ is kya, one. Small っ marks a held consonant before the next sound: きて (kite) differs from きって (kitte). Do not replace っ with full-size つ.

Long vowels last two morae. Keep written vowels: おおきい is o-o-ki-i. In many ordinary words, おう is pronounced with a long o and えい with a long e, while spelling remains おう and えい. You will meet the exact spelling with each word; do not change it on the basis of the Roman letters.

## Katakana

Katakana commonly writes loanwords, foreign names and emphatic forms. It is another script, not another language. Learn each new word's meaning separately; a loanword need not mean exactly what its source word means.

| vowel | ア a | イ i | ウ u | エ e | オ o |

ン is n. Voicing uses ガギグゲゴ, ザジズゼゾ, ダヂヅデド, バビブベボ and パピプペポ with the same values as the hiragana rows. Small ャュョ form combinations in the same way; small ッ holds the following consonant. Particles are short grammatical words attached to phrases. When は is the topic particle, read wa; the spelling stays は. The direction particle へ is read e, and the object particle を is read o. In other words the same signs may retain their usual sounds. The grammar note explains each particle when the story uses it.

Worked example: ゆいはかさをもちます。 Split for explanation only: ゆい | は | かさ | を | もちます. Read yu-i wa ka-sa o mo-chi-ma-su. It means “Yui holds an umbrella.” The story itself keeps ordinary unspaced Japanese.

Try three recognition questions with the table available, then uncover the answers. (1) Which name ends with ん: ゆい or れん? (2) Which means big: おおきい or ちいさい? (3) In ゆいは, is は read ha or wa? Answers: (1) れん; (2) おおきい; (3) wa, because it is the topic particle. This short decoding practice supplements the chapter's full exercises.

## Later kanji and typing

The opening four chapters use kana. Later, known words acquire kanji spellings with small kana readings above them, called furigana. A compound may need one reading over the whole word. You are not expected to guess a new reading from a character's appearance, and readings do not replace meaning support.

Use a Japanese input method (IME) to type answers. Convert to the taught spelling when a kanji form is requested; otherwise the item explains which variants it accepts. Preserve voicing, small kana and long vowels. Space and final punctuation are presentation differences; か/が and きや/きゃ can distinguish different words. You may consult the charts throughout the course.

The small kana above each complete word gives its authored reading every time. Keep using those readings; unaided kanji recall is optional. No new meaning follows merely from recognising a character.

Read the short meaning/reading packet below before the route. In these polite forms, いきます is “go”, きます is “come”, and かえります is “return”. Read the paper map as a document and compare its labels with the public street signs. Keep track of which labels the characters use for their next action. The unnamed adult woman running the shop is a new speaker, separate from Mei. みせのひと means the person at/running the shop here. She remains with customers while Yui and Ren can carry a delivery. The story keeps the original public note posted at the shop; Yui has its morning information on her own memo.

あります / ありません contrasts “is present” / “is not present”; います / いません is the corresponding pair for people. のみません means “do not drink.” のみませんか can invite: “Would you like a drink?” のみましょう proposes “Let’s drink.” Read the whole polite forms; do not derive dictionary forms or past forms yet. もちましょう can be an offer, “I’ll carry it,” when the speaker volunteers. に marks the recipient in かみをゆいにわたします, “hand the paper to Yui,” and the person met in かぎのかかりにあいます, “meet the key holder.”

The address field will use abstract writing lines: its exact address is not transcribed. Known route clues are not a substitute for a postal address. New story spellings of already known words correspond to いりぐち, あかい, あおい and なか, using five new characters; authored readings remain visible on every kanji. The practice and cards stay in kana.

The suffix にち belongs to calendar dates here. Learn the two complete readings above; they do not supply all date readings, a number series, or lengths of time. This fictional autumn story now places yesterday on the 12th and today on the 13th. The earlier relative days keep their order. The former-name expression まえのなまえ was already introduced in chapter 6 and is recalled here.

Polite past affirmative forms replace the final ます with ました: うけとります → うけとりました, “receive → received.” The corresponding past negative ends in ませんでした: あけませんでした means “did not open.” These are taught as complete polite forms. Yesterday does not mechanically force every sentence into past tense: a date identification still uses です. The chapter contrasts actions yesterday with intended actions today.

The opening is the morning after the shop visit. Chapter 6 stopped before a completed delivery; earlier actions are now told retrospectively. Past tense lets the speakers establish when each object moved and who received it. Follow the actual sequence and custody rather than assuming that every parcel or envelope mentioned is the same object.

The known whole time さんじ and its half-hour element acquire natural written spellings, with visible authored readings; the known go/come words also receive spellings. えほん is the complete word for a picture book; え means a picture. うた is a song and うたいます means sing. おおきいこえ/ちいさいこえ means a loud/soft voice here.
